periods.activity_title: Entering the Poem: A Bird's World Revealed

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.85): recite all four stanzas aloud together.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the poem's title and asks students what they imagine a bird might think about its world. A brief oral sharing of two or three responses warms up listening before the text is opened.

Teacher reads the poem aloud once, clearly and unhurriedly, while students follow in their textbooks (p.85–86). Teacher then reads each stanza a second time, pausing for students to mark any unfamiliar words.

Under “Let us read,” students recite the poem aloud together with the teacher, stanza by stanza. Teacher models the tone shift from certainty in stanza one to wonder in stanza four, and students echo the reading.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem moves through four distinct tones — confident, cosy, humbled, and philosophically open — and a choral read-aloud is the best moment to let students feel that arc before analysis begins. Watch for students who mumble through the last stanza; that stanza carries the poem's central wisdom and deserves the slowest, clearest delivery. Words like “fledgling” and “labours” may need a quick gloss drawn from the poem's context rather than a dictionary definition.

periods.activity_title: Mapping Each Stanza: Main Idea and Evidence

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.87): match each stanza to its main idea, two extra options given.
Let us discuss (p.88): decide whether two statements about the poem are true or false.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.87): match each of the four pictures to the correct poem line.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits the poem's four-stanza arc, asking one student to name what the bird lives in during each stanza. This oral recap anchors the class in the poem's structure before the matching task.

Under “Let us discuss,” students work through the stanza-to-main-idea matching task on p.87. Teacher reads all six options aloud, pairs discuss which two are extra and why, then the class agrees on answers together.

Still under “Let us discuss,” teacher reads the two True / False statements on p.88 aloud. Students decide individually, then share with a partner before the class settles on verified answers with textual evidence.

Teacher sets the picture-matching task on p.87 as home reading — students look at the four pictures and find the matching poem line for each, to be ready for quick sharing. Teacher clarifies what each picture shows.

periods.teacher_notes: The matching task on p.87 has two decoy options that test whether students have read carefully; the most common error is choosing option 3 (“the bird becomes blind due to leaves”) because the word “blind” appears in the poem, but the poem's meaning is figurative. Encourage students to read the option alongside the stanza before committing. For the True / False task, the statement about neighbours is a productive point of open discussion because the poem itself is ambiguous on who the neighbours are.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading: Straw Nest and Leaves

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.88): three sub-questions on the straw-nest stanza.
Let us think and reflect (p.88): three sub-questions on the leaves-and-blindness stanza.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads stanzas two and three of the poem aloud once more, slowly. Students follow on p.85–86 and underline the words “nestled,” “blind,” and “fluttered” as the teacher reads.

Under “Let us think and reflect,” teacher leads the class through the three questions on the straw-nest lines on p.88 — who lived in the nest, why the bird thought the world was straw, and which word shows the bird was comfortable. Students answer orally first, then in writing.

Teacher moves to the leaves-and-blindness extract on p.88 and guides the class through all three sub-questions: why the bird thought the world was leaves, what “I said” means in context, and completing the fill-in-blank sentence. Pairs compare their fill-in answers before a whole-class check.
Teacher draws a quick two-column table on the board — “What the bird saw” and “What it thought” — and invites two or three students to contribute one row each from today's extracts.

periods.teacher_notes: Both extracts on p.88 test whether students understand figurative language: the bird's world is not literally straw or leaves, but what it could perceive from where it was. A common pitfall is students treating “I said” as literal speech; the guided questions help redirect this. The poem's appreciation notes that “nestled” is the key comfort word, so if students are unsure during the third sub-question of the first extract, pointing them back to that word in the stanza is sufficient.
materials: Textbook open to p.85–86 and p.88

periods.activity_title: Thinking Deeper: Why the Bird Saw What It Saw

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.88): why the baby bird's world was small, round and blue.
Let us think and reflect (p.89): where the bird went after it fluttered from the nest.
Let us think and reflect (p.89): discuss who the bird's neighbours might be and why.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.89): write the quality the bird says it had when it flew away.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads stanza one aloud and poses the question from p.88: why did the baby bird think its world was small, round, and blue? Students think individually for a brief moment, then share responses; teacher confirms using the poem's own image of the egg-shell.
Teacher reads stanza three and asks the question from p.89: where did the bird go after it fluttered from the nest? Students locate the answer in the poem text and write it in one sentence.

For the neighbours discussion on p.89, teacher invites students to speculate freely: who might the bird's neighbours be, and why would they also not know how the world is made? Small groups share one idea each; teacher connects responses to the poem's theme of shared wonder and expanding perception.

Teacher frames the home-reading task: students are to find and write the quality the bird names on p.89 when it flies away, in one sentence of their own. Teacher reads the relevant stanza line aloud to anchor them.

periods.teacher_notes: The egg-shell question anchors the poem's central metaphor: the bird's knowledge was bounded by its physical environment at each stage. Students sometimes answer “because the bird liked blue” — redirect them to what the shell itself looks like. The neighbours question is intentionally open; the poem says they share the bird's uncertainty, so any reasonable answer naming other birds, creatures, or even humans is defensible and worth celebrating.
materials: Textbook open to p.85–86 and p.88–89

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.87): answer four word-clue blanks using words from the poem.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud once from p.85–86, with students joining in on every line they remember. This repeated reading consolidates the four-stanza arc and prepares students for careful word work.

Under “Let us discuss,” students work through the four word-clue blanks on p.87 — the shape of the first house, what the nest was made of, what the bird saw outside, and what it did at the end. Each answer is a word from the poem; pairs check against the text before the class confirms.

Students recite the poem stanza by stanza, this time without looking at the book for stanzas one and two. Teacher invites volunteers to recite a full stanza solo; classmates listen and echo the final line of each.
Teacher invites one student to say, in a single sentence, which stage of the bird's life they find most interesting and why. Two or three quick responses close the unit on a reflective note.

periods.teacher_notes: The word-clue blanks on p.87 use a letter-grid format; students sometimes guess without returning to the poem. Insisting that they point to the line in the text before writing the answer is good practice. The recitation in this unit is best approached as a confidence exercise, not a test — praising partial recall warmly encourages those who are still unsure.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.90): fill missing words while listening to the Paro parrot poem.

time_bands.activity: Teacher tells students they will listen to a short poem about a parrot named Paro. Students open their textbooks to p.90 and look at the fill-in task so they know which words to listen for.
Teacher reads the Paro poem aloud at a natural pace, twice. On the first reading students simply listen; on the second they write in the missing words in the gaps on p.90.
Teacher reads the poem a third time, slowly, and students verify their answers. Pairs compare what they wrote; teacher then reads each gapped line and confirms the correct word.

Teacher asks two quick oral questions grounded in the poem: what does Paro do in the morning, and what does the poem say the bird sees among the trees? Students answer aloud in one sentence each, connecting Paro's world to the bird's expanding world in the main poem.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening poem on p.90 is short and its vocabulary is accessible, but students may mishear “bright” as “bright” spelled differently or miss “stories” entirely on first hearing — the third read-through is essential for self-correction. Connecting Paro's morning flights to the main poem's bird venturing beyond the tree gives the listening task thematic weight rather than treating it as an isolated exercise.

periods.activity_title: If I Were a Bird: Speaking in Role

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.90): present yourself as the bird you would like to be.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the five prompt points from “Let us speak” on p.90 aloud and models a brief example using an imaginary bird. Students note that each point is a sentence starter: “I am…”, “I live in…”, and so on.

Students choose their bird and organise five points — appearance, home, daily activity, a message to humans — in a quick mental or written outline. Teacher circulates and offers a word or phrase to any student who is stuck on vocabulary.

Students present in turn, in small groups of four. Each presenter stands and speaks for a comfortable stretch; listeners note one thing they liked and one question they want to ask. After each group, one volunteer from each group presents to the whole class.

Teacher draws together two or three recurring ideas from the presentations — kinds of birds chosen, messages to humans — and links them back to the poem's theme that each creature knows only the world it inhabits.

periods.teacher_notes: The speaking task on p.90 scaffolds the presentation through five sentence-starters, which makes it accessible to hesitant speakers; encourage those students to use the starters as written rather than improvise from scratch. The “message for humans” prompt is the most imaginative and can draw on the poem's concern for nature — validate responses that echo the bird's growing awareness of a wider world.

periods.activity_title: Seeing the World Through Other Eyes

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.91): five sentences each on how the world looks to a baby and to a fish.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the model paragraph on p.91 aloud — how the poem's bird perceived its world — and asks: what makes this paragraph convincing? Students name one or two features: first-person voice, sensory detail, limited viewpoint.

Class discusses the baby and the fish as a whole group: what does a baby actually see, hear, or feel? What does a fish's world consist of? Teacher writes four or five key words on the board for each, drawn from students' suggestions, to serve as a word bank.

Students write five sentences for the baby and five for the fish in their notebooks, using the board word bank and the model paragraph on p.91 as guides. Teacher circulates, prompting students who use generic phrases to add a concrete sensory detail. Students then read their baby sentences to a partner and swap notebooks to check for sense.

Two volunteers read one sentence each — one from the baby paragraph and one from the fish paragraph — to the class. Teacher offers brief appreciation and notes one quality that made each sentence vivid.

periods.teacher_notes: The writing task on p.91 is the first sustained independent writing in this unit, and the model paragraph is the most important scaffold — make sure students read it before writing, not after. A common weakness is sentences that describe the creature's biology rather than its perception: “a fish has scales” instead of “a fish sees the world as shimmering blue and green.” Prompt students back toward the first-person voice the poem uses.

periods.activity_title: Rhyme and Description: Language at Work

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.89): complete rhyming-word table for all four stanzas and finish the new stanza.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.90): write six sentences using the describing words and the birdhouse picture.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the four rhyming pairs from the poem aloud — well/shell, other/mother, find/blind, labours/neighbours — and asks students what they notice about where each pair sits in its stanza. Students identify the second and fourth lines as the rhyming positions.

Under “Let us learn,” students complete the rhyming-words table on p.89: they fill in the pairs for stanzas two, three, and four, then add at least one new rhyming word for each stanza. Pairs share their additions and the class votes on the most inventive new words.

Students complete the new stanza on p.89 — filling in the two rhyming gaps (“know” and “best”). Teacher reads the completed stanza aloud and invites one or two students to suggest alternative rhymes that also work, discussing why some words fit and others do not.

Teacher previews the describing-words task on p.90 for home reading — students look at the birdhouse picture and the eight adjectives listed, and write six sentences using those words. Teacher clarifies the task and confirms that students know what each adjective means.

periods.teacher_notes: The rhyme-table task on p.89 is straightforward for stanzas one through three, but “labours / neighbours” in stanza four may puzzle students because neither word looks like a typical rhyme pair at first glance — draw attention to the shared “-ours” ending. The new-stanza completion has a single correct answer for the gaps as printed, but accepting other valid rhymes warmly rewards students who engage creatively with the language.

periods.activity_title: From Shells to Homes: Materials and Meaning

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.91): list home materials, discuss why not straw, and explore home vs house.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to close their eyes and picture their own home, then name two materials they can see in it. Responses are collected on the board; teacher notes the variety and connects back to the poem's bird whose first home was pale-blue shell and whose next was straw.

Under “Let us explore” on p.91, students make a quick written list of materials their home is made of, then the class discusses why human homes are not built of straw — covering durability, weather, and safety. Teacher invites students to share one reason each.

Students discuss in groups: if they could build a home from any materials, what would they choose and why? Groups share one imaginative choice with a reason. Teacher then poses the question from p.91: how is a home different from a house? The class arrives at a shared distinction through discussion.

Teacher briefly notes the second part of “Let us explore” on p.92 — different kinds of bird nests and the workers who build human homes — as an observation task students can pursue independently. No collected work is required.

periods.teacher_notes: The home-versus-house distinction on p.91 is the conceptual heart of this unit: a house is a structure, a home is a place of belonging — which connects directly to the poem's warmth around the nest and the mother. Students from varied living situations should feel that every genuine shelter counts as a home; keep the discussion affirming. The materials list can remain personal and need not be shared aloud unless students choose to.

periods.activity_title: Bird Nests, Human Builders, and Community Workers

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.92): complete the workers-and-their-work table and add two extra workers.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens p.92 and shows students the workers table. The example — mason lays bricks and stones — is read aloud. Teacher asks: what is the difference between a mason and an architect? Students share initial ideas before looking at the list.

Under “Let us explore” on p.92, students work individually or in pairs to complete the table: painter, electrician, plumber, carpenter, and architect, writing one sentence of work description for each. Teacher circulates and prompts students who are unsure — for instance, what a plumber works with, or what an electrician installs.

Each pair adds two workers of their own choosing to the table and writes a work description for each. The class shares their additions; teacher collects the range on the board — interior designer, gardener, tiler, and so on — and discusses which workers a bird's nest needs and which it does not, connecting back to the poem's image of the straw nest.

Teacher invites students to note, in one sentence in their notebook, which worker they think is most important to building a safe home and why. Two or three responses are shared aloud to close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may know the workers by their local-language names but not the English terms — accepting the local term and writing the English alongside it builds vocabulary without embarrassment. The connection between bird nest-building and human construction is the imaginative thread: birds are their own architects and masons, which gives the community-workers task a surprising depth when that parallel is pointed out.

periods.activity_title: The Bird's Journey, Our Journey: A Whole-Chapter Reflection

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the full poem aloud from p.85–86, stanza by stanza, and asks students to listen for the single word in each stanza that best describes the bird's feeling — small, cosy, humbled, wondering. Students share their chosen words and the class agrees on one per stanza.

Teacher leads a whole-class discussion connecting the poem's four stages to human experience: how does growing up change what we think we know? Students draw on the poem's metaphor — shell, nest, leaves, open sky — to frame their own ideas. Three or four students contribute a thought each.

Students write freely for a sustained stretch: they choose the stanza that feels most true to where they are in life right now, copy its two rhyming lines, and write two or three sentences explaining their choice. This is individual, in their notebooks, with no sharing required.

Teacher closes by reading the poem's final stanza once more — “I don't know how the world is made / And neither do my neighbours” — and invites one volunteer to share what they find beautiful or surprising about that ending. The unit ends on the poem's own note of open-ended wonder.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws together the poem's central theme — that perception grows with experience and that mature wisdom admits what it does not know — as discussed through reading, speaking, writing, and the beyond-text explorations of homes and community. Any student encountering the poem for the first time in this unit has everything they need; the poem itself is the only text required. The writing task begins and ends here: students choose, copy, and reflect, all within the unit's own minutes.

items.source_lo: Student reads, comprehends, and interprets a poem's meaning across its stanzas using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four-stanza poem tracing a bird's expanding perception from egg to open sky.
items.item_stem: In the poem “What a Bird Thought,” the bird lives in four different places across the four stanzas. Which of the following correctly names all four places in the order the bird experiences them?

what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student reversed the first two stages, placing the nest before the shell.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student confused the order of the nest and the tree, skipping the nest-to-tree sequence.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Replaces the nest with “leaves,” conflating the stanza three image with a stage of the bird's home.

items.source_lo: Student reads, comprehends, and interprets a poem's meaning across its stanzas using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four-stanza poem tracing a bird's expanding perception from egg to open sky.
items.item_stem: In the final stanza, the bird says it does not know how the world is made, and that its neighbours share this uncertainty. What does this ending reveal about the poem's central idea, and how does the bird's attitude in this stanza differ from its attitude in stanza one? Give your answer in two or three sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The final stanza shows that the more the bird experiences, the more it realises how much it does not know — a sign of growing wisdom rather than failure. In stanza one the bird was confident that its tiny, pale-blue world was the whole world; in stanza four it accepts with openness that the world is too large and complex to be fully understood. The tone shifts from certainty to philosophical wonder.

items.source_lo: Student listens attentively to a spoken poem and retrieves specific words using a listening poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Short poem about Paro the parrot flying and seeing the world; five missing words to fill.
items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the poem about Paro the parrot aloud. Listen carefully and decide whether each statement below is true or false.

options.text: Paro flies among mountains where the breeze is light.
Paro spreads its wings in the evening.
Paro's feathers are described as bright.
The poem invites the listener to travel through blue skies.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the poem says “my feathers are bright and they glow.”
2. False — the poem says Paro spreads its wings in the morning, not the evening.
3. True — the poem says “come with me through the skies so blue.”
4. False — the poem places Paro among trees, not mountains.

items.source_lo: Student listens attentively to a spoken poem and retrieves specific words using a listening poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Short poem about Paro the parrot flying and seeing the world; five missing words to fill.
items.item_stem: After listening to the poem about Paro the parrot, answer the following question in one or two sentences: Paro says there are “many new stories” among the trees. What does this suggest about what Paro finds when it flies — and how is this similar to what the bird in the main poem discovers when it first ventures out of its nest?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Paro finds that flying through the world reveals new and surprising things — stories, sights, and places — suggesting that the world is richer than it appears from one spot. This is similar to the bird in the main poem discovering leaves when it first fluttered out, realising that the world was far bigger and more varied than its shell or nest had shown.

items.source_lo: Student delivers a structured first-person oral presentation using a role-play speaking task as the vehicle.
items.source_context: First-person oral presentation as a chosen bird: appearance, home, daily life, message to humans.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are a bird of your choice. In two or three sentences, describe what you look like and where you live. Speak clearly in the first person.

expected_elements: Names the chosen bird and uses “I am” to introduce it.
Describes at least one physical feature — colour, size, or a body part.
Names the bird's home or habitat with a brief detail.
Speaks in complete sentences at a pace the class can follow.

items.source_lo: Student delivers a structured first-person oral presentation using a role-play speaking task as the vehicle.
items.source_context: First-person oral presentation as a chosen bird: appearance, home, daily life, message to humans.
items.item_stem: Still speaking as the bird you chose, give a short message to the humans who share your world. Tell them one thing you wish they understood about your life or your home, and give a reason for your wish. Speak for four to six sentences.

expected_elements: States one clear wish or message addressed to humans.
Gives a reason connected to the bird's life or habitat.
Maintains the first-person bird voice throughout.
Uses appropriate tone — persuasive, gentle, or urgent — and complete sentences.

items.source_lo: Student writes an imaginative first-person perspective piece using a guided writing task as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Five-sentence perspective paragraphs — how the world looks to a baby and to a fish.
items.item_stem: A baby sees the world from a very small and close-up view — much like the bird in the egg saw only pale blue shell. Write a short paragraph of four sentences describing what the world might look, sound, or feel like to a baby. Write in the first person, as though you are the baby.

expected_elements: Writes in the first person using “I see / feel / hear.”
Includes at least one sensory detail — sight, sound, or touch.
Describes a limited or close-up view of the world.
Uses four complete sentences with correct punctuation.

items.source_lo: Student writes an imaginative first-person perspective piece using a guided writing task as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Five-sentence perspective paragraphs — how the world looks to a baby and to a fish.
items.item_stem: The poem's bird discovers at the end that it cannot fully understand the world — and neither can its neighbours. Write a short paragraph of five sentences from the point of view of a fish, explaining what the world looks like from inside the water. Then add one final sentence in which the fish admits something about the world that it does not understand. Write in the first person.

expected_elements: Writes five perspective sentences in the first person as the fish.
Describes the underwater world with at least one specific sensory image.
Final sentence expresses something the fish finds puzzling or unknowable.
Connects implicitly or explicitly to the idea of limited perception.
Uses complete sentences and maintains first-person voice throughout.

items.source_lo: Student identifies rhyme patterns and uses descriptive adjectives accurately using vocabulary activities as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rhyming pairs across four stanzas (well/shell, other/mother, find/blind, labours/neighbours) and describing adjectives.
items.item_stem: The poem uses adjectives such as “pale,” “little,” and “round” to help readers picture the bird’s world at each stage. Choose any two of these adjectives from the poem and write one original sentence for each, using the adjective to describe something from the natural world — not from the poem itself. Then explain, in one sentence, what each adjective adds to the picture.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Answers will vary. An acceptable response uses each chosen adjective correctly to describe a natural object — for example, “A pale moon hung over the river” — and follows it with a sentence explaining that “pale” suggests the moon’s faint, washed-out colour. Full credit requires that each sentence is original, the adjective is grammatically placed before a noun or after a linking verb, and the explanation names a quality the adjective conveys.

items.source_lo: Student connects a literary theme to real-world structures and community roles using an interdisciplinary exploration as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Home materials, home versus house distinction, bird nests, and community construction workers.
items.item_stem: The bird in the poem moves from a shell to a straw nest to the open sky. Think about the materials humans use to build their homes. Write an extended response (one paragraph of five to six sentences) in which you: (a) name three materials commonly used to build human homes, (b) explain why each material is more durable or safer than straw, and (c) explain, in your final sentence, what you think the difference is between a house and a home.

expected_elements: Names three real building materials — brick, concrete, wood, or similar.
Gives a reason for each material's advantage over straw — strength, weather resistance, fire safety.
Final sentence distinguishes house (structure) from home (place of belonging and comfort).
Response is written in complete sentences and organised logically.

items.source_lo: Student connects a literary theme to real-world structures and community roles using an interdisciplinary exploration as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Home materials, home versus house distinction, bird nests, and community construction workers.
items.item_stem: Birds build their nests entirely on their own — the poem's bird needed no carpenter, no plumber, and no architect. Humans, by contrast, rely on many skilled workers. Choose any three of these workers — painter, electrician, plumber, carpenter, architect — and complete the project task below: (a) Write one sentence describing what each chosen worker does when building or finishing a home. (b) For each worker, write one sentence explaining what would go wrong in a home if that worker's job were not done. Present your work as a small table with three rows.

expected_elements: Names three workers from the given list with accurate job descriptions.
Each consequence sentence is realistic and specific to that worker's role.
Work is presented in a clear three-row table format.
Writing uses complete sentences and correct capitalisation.
